4.text: The products of reindeer-breeding were then of very slight importance, while at

5.text: present they amount to about three-fifths of the total Anui purchases. The

6.text: fair took place in the spring, and lasted three days; it was held in the open,

7.text: before the gates of the Russian fort, sometimes even farther away on the ice

8.text: of the river. The Chukchee came fully armed with spears, bows and arrows,

9.text: and large knives tied to their belts. Altercations and brawls, and even

10.text: bloodshed, were not uncommon because of disagreements about prices. There-

11.text: fore in 1812 Gen. Treskin, the governor of Irkutsk, who also ruled the Yakutsk

12.text: province (i. e., northeastern Siberia as far as Chaun Bay and the Anadyr

13.text: River), ordered that trade in tobacco, the principal commodity, which was

14.text: bartered by the Russians for beavers, foxes, martens, and walrus-tusks brought

15.text: by the natives, should be conducted on terms fixed beforehand by the chief

16.text: officer, with the advice of prominent merchants. The prices were fixed annually

17.text: by the common consent of the merchants, and iron and copper kettles were

18.text: often included in the list of commodities with fixed price.

19.text: At the usual rate, one pud (thirty-six pounds Avoirdupois) of tobacco or

20.text: of iron kettles was equal to ten red foxes, and one pud of copper kettles

21.text: was equal to twenty foxes. In later years a wolverine-skin or a large kettle,

22.text: was given in addition to the large tobacco-bags of three puds each, which

23.text: were valued at sixty fox-skins. The value of other peltries was expressed in

24.text: red-fox units. For instance, four white foxes were equal to one red fox, one

25.text: gray fox or one beaver was equal to two red foxes, one black fox was equal

26.text: to twenty red foxes, etc. The details of these rules were oppressive to the

27.text: small traders, who were punished for the slightest infraction. In several

28.text: instances even the richer merchants forfeited their right to trade with the

29.text: Chukchee by accepting a seal-skin as the equivalent of a single missing paw

30.text: in a lot of many hundred red-fox skins. The fox-skin should have had all

31.text: four paws to be worth a price in tobacco. In the sixties of the last century,

32.text: with the decline of the fair, the rules began to go out of use, and in 1869

33.text: they were abolished by Baron von Maydell.
